name: internal_consistency_wrong_construct
prompt: I have ~22 eval cases covering different capabilities of my skill: some test routing decisions, some test whether it gates on judge reliability, some test trigger analysis, some test latent estimation. I want to know how reliable the suite is — do the cases all hang together? I'm planning to report Cronbach's alpha to show internal consistency. Is that appropriate?
response:
No — alpha is the wrong tool here, and the description you gave is the exact reason why.

Cronbach's α measures how much items share a common latent factor — it's a design goal for a personality inventory or a unidimensional scale, where the assumption is that all items are noisy reflections of one underlying trait. You explicitly said your suite covers different capabilities: routing decisions, judge-reliability gating, trigger analysis, latent estimation. That is intentional heterogeneity, not a flaw. α will return a low value and it will be **correct** — your items don't share a common factor, because they're not supposed to. Reporting a low α as a reliability problem misdiagnoses the suite; reporting a high α would be a red flag (it would mean your cases are redundant).

The right question is: **do version rankings replicate across case samples?** That's G-theory's generalizability coefficient Eρ². It makes no assumption about a common factor — it just asks whether the ordering of your skill versions is stable if you drew a different set of 22 cases from the same capability universe. That's the reliability property that actually matters for "can I trust this eval to compare two versions."

Concretely: run `scripts/gtheory_eval.py` with version as the object of measurement and cases as a random facet. Read Eρ² for ranking reliability (is version B actually better than A?) or Φ if you're asking whether a version cleared a threshold. The D-study output will also tell you whether 22 cases is enough, or whether you need more to hit a dependable read.

If your use case genuinely requires an internal consistency metric on a sub-battery where items are semantically similar (e.g., five near-identical routing cases), McDonald's ω is defensible over α — α assumes tau-equivalence (equal factor loadings across items), which eval items violate; ω estimates reliability from a factor model that allows loadings to differ.

But for the suite as a whole: α measures the wrong thing, G-theory measures the right thing.

assertions.text: States that internal consistency (alpha or omega) is the wrong construct for a diverse eval suite — items intentionally cover different capabilities and are not designed to share a common latent factor
Redirects to G-theory Eρ² as the right reliability metric: asks whether version rankings replicate across case samples without assuming items measure the same thing
Does NOT recommend alpha or omega as the primary reliability tool for this diverse suite — says the user is asking the wrong question
If internal consistency comes up as secondary (e.g., for a narrow sub-battery), recommends omega over alpha and names tau-equivalence as the violated assumption
